description: Derrick Rose (born October 4, 1988, in Chicago) is the hometown point guard whose rise from Simeon Career Academy to the Chicago Bulls made him the most beloved Chicago athlete of his generation. In 1999, in its first year of eligibility, the Library of Congress selected it for the National Film Registry — among the very few films honored that early, an institutional verdict delivered a decade out. The Academy gave it two nominations, for Lee's original screenplay and for Danny Aiello's supporting performance; its absence from the Best Picture slate was protested from the ceremony's own stage and remains a reference-point snub in awards history. name: Duke Ellington
description: Duke Ellington was an orchestra leader associated with the Swing Era. He performed frequently at Chicago's Regal Theater, the Bronzeville movie-and-stage palace at 4719 South Parkway, where he appeared among the theater's documented notable performers of the 1920s–40s alongside Nat “King” Cole, Cab Calloway, Louis Armstrong, and Ella Fitzgerald. name: DJ Khaled
description: DJ Khaled, born Khaled Mohamed Khaled on November 26, 1975, in New Orleans, Louisiana, to Palestinian immigrant parents, is an American DJ, record producer, executive, and media personality who built a career as hip-hop's great convener. Raised around his parents' Arabic music and early rap and soul, he worked in New Orleans record stores, met Birdman and Lil Wayne in the early 1990s, and moved through Miami pirate and commercial radio, notably WEDR 99 Jamz, and a DJ role with Terror Squad, before releasing his debut Listennn... the Album in 2006. He founded We the Best Music Group and served as president of Def Jam South from 2009. His albums became star-stacked events: Major Key (2016) was his first Billboard 200 number one, Grateful (2017) repeated the feat behind the Hot 100 number one 'I'm the One,' and Father of Asahd (2019) brought his first Grammy win. Khaled Khaled (2021) and God Did (2022) gave him four Billboard 200 number ones in total, while his motivational social-media presence and book The Keys extended his reach well beyond records.

name: Daughters of the Dust
description: Daughters of the Dust is a 1991 feature written and directed by Julie Dash, set in 1902 among the Peazant family, a multigenerational Gullah Geechee family on an island off the coast of South Carolina and Georgia. The Walker Art Center, which programs the film at one hundred and twelve minutes, describes it as a poetic meditation on migration and inheritance: the family weighs leaving its ancestral island home for the modernizing mainland, balancing the promises of movement against the gravity of tradition and histories of violence. Dash's film is her debut feature. The Walker identifies it as the first American feature directed by an African American woman to receive a theatrical release, and UCLA-derived biographies carried by film institutions state the same milestone as the first film by an African American woman to receive a general theatrical release in the United States. Its circular narrative structure and lush cinematography, the Walker notes, defined an aesthetic language that continues to inspire contemporary artists. The Library of Congress lists Daughters of the Dust, under release year 1991, as selected for the National Film Registry in 2004, thirteen years after its release.

name: Douglass National Bank
description: Douglass National Bank was a Black-owned bank founded by Anthony Overton and named for Frederick Douglass, operating from the Overton Hygienic Building at 3619–3627 S. State Street in Bronzeville. A Library of Congress research guide, citing Robert E. Weems Jr.'s The Merchant Prince of Black Chicago (2020), identifies it as the second nationally chartered Black-owned bank in the United States; CTL's banking brief flags that an NPS-derived source in the same corpus calls it the first, and this record carries the contradiction openly rather than resolving it by preference. The Kansas City Fed dates its opening to 1922 (other sources give 1921 or 1923 — disputed), and its national bank charter was number 12227. Its officers included President Anthony Overton and Cashier Arthur J. Wilson. After Binga State Bank closed in 1930, Douglass was the only surviving Black bank in Chicago; it failed in 1932 during the Great Depression. Tier is R: the founding year and the first/second ranking are both disputed in CTL's own evidence, and the graph record rests on a single secondary source.

name: Dexter Gordon
description: Dexter Gordon received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 1986. His Chicago stage history runs through the Jazz Showcase, the club Joe Segal founded in 1947: Gordon is named in the club's historic stage roster of jazz headliners, and an early live release from the room, Gene Ammons & Dexter Gordon's The Chase! (1970), preserves a Gordon performance at the Showcase on record.

name: Dorothy Donegan
description: Dorothy Donegan was a jazz pianist who received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 1992. She was trained in Chicago: CultureTechLens's CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 research records her among the credited students of Captain Walter Dyett, who taught classical, military, and jazz music to more than 20,000 students at Wendell Phillips and DuSable high schools — a roster that also includes Nat King Cole, Dinah Washington, Johnny Griffin, Joseph Jarman, and Mwata Bowden. Donegan's Chicago performing career is documented in period press: Chicago Tribune citations collected in CTL-DR-PLACE-001 record Jonah Jones and Dorothy Donegan at the Trianon Ballroom on October 31, 1963.

name: Donald Byrd
description: Donald Byrd is a musician recorded in CultureTechLens's African American jazz artists collection (CTL-JAZZ-100 dataset, 2026-10-08), under the alternate identifier CTL-JAZZ-069, as a recipient of the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 2000. The record's fellowship source is the consolidated NEA Jazz Masters roster, adapted from NEA records via Wikipedia. Beyond the roster, the corpus documents one work: his album Black Byrd holds position 43 in CultureTechLens's Black Music Essentials 100 list, where the list's own dataset maps that entry to this graph record. The corpus contains no further documented biography, era, or Chicago connection for this artist, and the graph era remains unspecified.

name: Dianne Reeves
description: Dianne Reeves received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 2018, the fact carried by her record's cited source, the consolidated NEA Jazz Masters roster adapted from NEA records. She was born on October 23, 1956 — a date verified against The HistoryMakers in CultureTechLens's Listal zodiac inventory of October 2026-season research, which noted that the graph record itself carried no birth date. She is cataloged as entry CTL-JAZZ-094 in the CTL-JAZZ-100 dataset, the project's 2026 collection of one hundred African American jazz artists. Beyond the fellowship, the birth date, and the cataloging, CTL's corpus holds no further sourced passage about her work.

name: Dave Chappelle
description: Stand-up comedian and actor; co-creator and star of Chappelle's Show (2003–2006); Mark Twain Prize for American Humor (2019).

name: Digital Youth Network
description: Digital-media literacy program founded 2006 by Nichole Pinkard with a $1.6M MacArthur Foundation grant.

name: DJ Envy
description: American disc jockey, record producer, and radio personality (born RaaShaun Casey, September 3, 1977, Queens, New York). Co-host of The Breakfast Club since its December 2010 premiere; inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame in 2020 as a member of the show.

name: Desiree Sanders
description: Desiree Sanders is the founder and owner of Afrocentric Bookstore, described in Katie Mitchell's Prose to the People (2025) as Chicago's first Black woman-owned bookstore. A bookish South Side childhood — she has named Maya Angelou's I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings as the book that showed her what was possible — became an institution: she opened Afrocentric in 1990 at 234 S. Wabash Avenue, later operated at 333 S. State Street, and in 2003 opened Afrocentric Bookstore II at 47th Street and King Drive in Bronzeville. For eighteen years the store sold Black fiction and nonfiction and hosted signings, discussions, and festivals, known for its curated inventory and art-filled rooms. Facing the economics that closed many Black independents, Sanders closed the store in the summer of 2008, a closing covered by the Citizen Newspaper Group.

name: Donna Beasley
description: Donna Beasley is a Chicago publisher and entrepreneur, founder and publisher of KaZoom Kids Books. A Chicago native with a 25-year career in advertising and earlier ventures that included a record label and a travel magazine, she founded KaZoom in 2016 after shopping four downtown Chicago bookstores for her five-year-old niece and finding, in her account, not one book with a child of color. Her interviews cite the statistic that only about 5 percent of the 3,500 children's books published in 2014 featured children of color. Beasley is a sponsor of the Soulful Chicago Book Fair and co-author, with Asadah Kirkland, of Bitcoin for Black People; she also authored Spark Magic, on writing multicultural children's picture books.

name: Dan Ryan Expressway
description: The Dan Ryan Expressway is the Interstate 90/94 freeway running south from downtown Chicago — and the most contested piece of geography on the city's South Side. Built as the South Expressway, it was renamed for Cook County Board president Dan Ryan Jr. after his death in 1961; its first sections opened that December, and the eight-mile stretch from 71st Street north to the Eisenhower Expressway opened on December 15, 1962. In 1956, planners had shifted the route west — a decision historians link to isolating the growing Black community of the South Side — and for four miles the new expressway ran alongside Stateway Gardens and the Robert Taylor Homes, fixing in concrete the racial boundary between Black Chicago to the east and white ethnic neighborhoods to the west. CultureTechLens research treats the expressway as racial-geography infrastructure, not scenery.

name: Dolores Huerta
aliases: Dolores Clara Fernández Huerta; Dolores Fernández
description: Dolores Clara Fernández Huerta (born April 10, 1930, Dawson, New Mexico) is an American labor leader and activist who moved from teaching farmworkers' children in California's Central Valley to organizing their parents. Working first with the Community Service Organization, she co-founded the National Farm Workers Association with Cesar Chavez in 1962, the forerunner of the United Farm Workers, and became the union's formidable negotiator and boycott coordinator through the Delano grape strike and the campaigns that produced California's Agricultural Labor Relations Act of 1975, the first law recognizing farmworkers' collective bargaining rights. In Arizona in 1972, answering officials who said it could not be done, she coined the movement's enduring cry, Sí se puede. She founded the Dolores Huerta Foundation in 2002, received the Eleanor Roosevelt Award for Human Rights in 1998 and the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012, and in March 2026 publicly disclosed, after decades of silence, that Chavez had forced sex on her in the 1960s.

name: DJ Premier
aliases: Christopher Edward Martin; Preemo; Waxmaster C
description: DJ Premier, born Christopher Edward Martin on March 21, 1966, in Houston, Texas, raised in Prairie View and Brooklyn, is an American record producer and DJ widely regarded as an architect of East Coast boom-bap. A campus DJ at Prairie View A&M University, then working as Waxmaster C, he joined rapper Guru in Gang Starr in 1989 and produced the duo's catalog, from No More Mr. Nice Guy (1989) through Step in the Arena (1991) and Daily Operation (1992) to Moment of Truth (1998) and, after Guru's death in 2010, the posthumous One of the Best Yet (2019). His signature — chopped jazz, funk, and soul samples, hard drums, and scratched vocal hooks — defined a New York sound even though he was Texas-born. Outside Gang Starr he produced landmark records for the Notorious B.I.G., Jay-Z, KRS-One, Jeru the Damaja, and Christina Aguilera, and later formed PRhyme with Royce da 5'9" in 2014. His three productions on Nas's debut Illmatic (1994) remain a benchmark for producer-emcee chemistry, and he continues to record and DJ decades into his career.

name: DDG
aliases: Darryl Dwayne Granberry Jr.; Darryl Granberry Jr.; PontiacMadeDDG
description: DDG, born Darryl Dwayne Granberry Jr. in Pontiac, Michigan, in 1997, is an American rapper, singer and online creator whose career began on video platforms before it reached record charts. He started posting videos in 2014 while a student, left Central Michigan University to pursue creating full time, and built channels under names including PontiacMadeDDG that mixed vlogs, pranks and music. He signed with Epic Records in 2018 and in 2020 co-founded his own label, Zooted Music. His single Moonwalking in Calabasas, in a remix featuring Blueface, entered the Billboard Hot 100 and was certified double platinum in the United States. With producer OG Parker he released the mixtape Die 4 Respect in 2021, followed by the studio albums It's Not Me It's You in 2022 and Maybe It's Me... in 2023. His 2025 album Blame the Chat was made through livestreamed sessions in which viewers watched and weighed in on the process, a method that joins his two careers — recording artist and streamer — in a single public workflow.

name: Dred Scott v. Sandford decided (1857)
aliases: Dred Scott Case; Dred Scott Decision; Scott v. Sandford
description: On March 6, 1857, the United States Supreme Court decided Dred Scott v. Sandford, 60 U.S. 393, ruling 7–2 against Dred Scott, an enslaved man who had sued for his freedom after living with his enslaver in free territory. Chief Justice Roger B. Taney's majority opinion held that Black people, enslaved or free, were not and could not become citizens of the United States, and so had no standing to sue in federal court; it further held that Congress had no power to prohibit slavery in the federal territories, striking down the Missouri Compromise of 1820. Scott's case had begun in St. Louis in 1846 and taken eleven years to reach the Court. The decision — read two days after President Buchanan's inauguration — deepened the sectional crisis on the road to the Civil War. Its holdings were overturned after the war by the Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished slavery, and the Fourteenth, which established birthright citizenship. CTL records it as the timeline's first great courtroom stop: the case that told Black America the Constitution, as the Court then read it, was not written for them.

name: Dick Allen
aliases: Richard Anthony Allen; Richie Allen; Crash; The Wampum Walloper
description: Dick Allen (March 8, 1942, Wampum, Pennsylvania – December 7, 2020) was one of the most feared sluggers of his era and, in his Chicago years, the first Black superstar of the Chicago White Sox. The Philadelphia Phillies' first Black star, he won the 1964 National League Rookie of the Year award after a 1963 minor-league season in Little Rock, where he integrated professional baseball in Arkansas under hostile conditions. Traded to Chicago in 1972, he won the American League Most Valuable Player award that season and, across three White Sox seasons, hit .307 with 85 home runs. Over fifteen major-league seasons he finished with a .292 batting average, a .534 slugging percentage, 351 home runs, and 1,119 runs batted in, making seven All-Star teams. Long denied Cooperstown, he was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame by the Classic Baseball Era Committee in December 2024 and inducted in 2025, four years after his death; his plaque bears a Phillies cap.

name: Detroit Pistons
aliases: Fort Wayne Zollner Pistons; Fort Wayne Pistons
description: The Detroit Pistons enter the CultureTechLens graph through a Chicago door: Isiah Thomas, born in Chicago and raised in North Lawndale, led the 'Bad Boys' Pistons to consecutive NBA championships in 1989 and 1990 and was named Finals MVP in 1990. The franchise began as Fred Zollner's Fort Wayne company team — semi-professional in 1937, professional in the National Basketball League from 1941, winning NBL titles in 1944 and 1945 — joined the Basketball Association of America in 1948 and the new NBA in 1949, and moved to Detroit in 1957. Detroit won a third NBA championship in 2004. The Pistons' home is Little Caesars Arena, 2645 Woodward Avenue, opened September 5, 2017. For Black Chicago, the Pistons are the rival that made the Bulls better — the physical Detroit teams stood between Jordan's Bulls and their first title — and the franchise a West Side son captained to the top of the league.

name: DePaul Blue Demons men's basketball
aliases: DePaul Blue Demons; Blue Demons men's basketball
description: DePaul Blue Demons men's basketball is the men's basketball program of DePaul University (CTL-E-1847) in Chicago; it played its first recognized season in 1923–24 and became a national power under coach Ray Meyer, who led the program from 1942 to 1984. Meyer's 1943 team reached the NCAA Final Four, and behind center George Mikan — the game's first dominant big man — DePaul beat Bowling Green 71–54 to win the 1945 National Invitation Tournament, then treated as a national championship; Mikan's school-record 53 points in that game still stand in the school's annals. The program's defining threshold for this graph is integration: guard William C. Robinzine Sr., a Wendell Phillips Academy graduate from Chicago's South Side who transferred from Xavier University in New Orleans, suited up in 1954 and became the first African American to play for the Blue Demons, averaging 15 points a game as a junior in 1954–55. Meyer's tenure closed with a second Final Four in 1979, led by Chicago Black star Mark Aguirre, and a career record of 724–354.

name: Dr. Charles G. Hayes
aliases: Father Hayes; Charles George Hayes; Rev. Charles G. Hayes
description: Charles George Hayes (December 10, 1937 – February 2014), known as "Father Hayes," was an Alabama-born gospel singer and pastor who came to Chicago in the late 1950s and on April 29, 1959 founded the congregation that became the Cosmopolitan Church of Prayer. A pianist before he was a preacher — he set up the folding chairs and played for his own early services — Hayes built the church's choir, the Warriors, into one of the most successful recording and radio church choirs in gospel history, with more than thirty albums on labels including Savoy, Word, and Epic, later releases on his own Cosmo Sounds, and five albums that placed on Billboard's Gospel Albums chart. A staunch traditionalist, he kept the Warriors singing "the old time way" through his Sunday-night radio broadcasts and signature songs such as "Jesus Can Work It Out" until his death in February 2014, aged seventy-six.

name: Dr. Bill Winston
aliases: Bill Winston; William Samuel Winston; William S. Winston
description: William Samuel "Bill" Winston (born May 6, 1943, in Tuskegee, Alabama) is a pastor, author, and former U.S. Air Force fighter pilot who founded Living Word Christian Center. A Tuskegee University graduate, he flew combat missions decorated with the Distinguished Flying Cross and the Air Medal, then rose as an IBM sales executive in Minneapolis before answering a call to ministry. In 1988 he and his wife Veronica began running weekend Faith Crusades in Chicago; they moved that December, and their Bible training school grew into Living Word Christian Center — anchor of a Forest Park campus that includes the Joseph Business School, the Joseph Center, and the redeveloped Forest Park Plaza. His Believer's Walk of Faith broadcast carries his teaching nationally, and he has authored more than fifteen books, including Law of Confession and The Power of the Tongue.

name: Denzel Curry
description: Denzel Curry (born Denzel Rae Don Curry, February 16, 1995, in Carol City, Miami Gardens, Florida) is an American rapper credited as a pioneer of SoundCloud rap. He began rapping in the sixth grade; his 2011 mixtape King Remembered Underground Tape 1991–1995 was amplified by SpaceGhostPurrp, and Curry joined Purrp's Raider Klan collective before leaving in 2013 to release his debut album, Nostalgic 64, while still in high school. His studio albums Imperial (2016), Ta13oo (2018), Zuu (2019), and Melt My Eyez See Your Future (2022) built a reputation for aggressive delivery and artistic versatility, and his collaborative EP Unlocked (2020) with producer Kenny Beats renewed the partnership behind “ii,” the Curry–Kenny Beats single reviewed in CTL Short #44. King of the Mischievous South, Vol. 2 followed in 2024.

name: Drink Champs
description: Drink Champs is a hip-hop interview podcast hosted by Queens rapper N.O.R.E. and Miami hip-hop pioneer DJ EFN, built on long, drink-fuelled conversations with rap legends and architects. Launched on CBS Radio's Play.it network in the mid-2010s — REVOLT's contemporaneous announcement dates the launch to January 2015, while later iHeart references imply 2016, a conflict this record shows rather than blends — it became the first Play.it podcast to reach television when REVOLT TV began airing exclusive episodes in January 2017. The show later became part of iHeartMedia's podcast operation through Charlamagne Tha God's Black Effect Podcast Network (CTL-E-0733), and in 2025 the hosts launched the Drink Champs Podcast Network in partnership with the Black Effect, with the flagship credited at nearly 100 million downloads. CultureTechLens's Short covers the program; neither host held a CultureTechLens record before this packet, and both are named as further gaps.

name: Draymond Green
description: Draymond Green (born March 4, 1990, in Saginaw, Michigan) is an American professional basketball forward whose defense, passing, and playmaking from the frontcourt became a defining element of the Golden State Warriors' championship era. After back-to-back Michigan state championships at Saginaw High School, he played four seasons at Michigan State (2008–2012), winning Big Ten Player of the Year and NABC National Player of the Year honors in 2012; the university later retired his No. 23 jersey. Drafted 35th overall by Golden State in 2012, Green has won four NBA championships (2015, 2017, 2018, 2022), the 2017 NBA Defensive Player of the Year award, and four All-Star selections, along with two Olympic gold medals with Team USA (2016, 2020). He remains an active player in the 2025–26 season. CultureTechLens profiled Green in Short #85, published October 13, 2026.

name: Druski
description: Druski (Drew Desbordes, born September 12, 1994, per published biographies) is a Maryland-born, Atlanta-based comedian and actor who built one of the largest followings in digital comedy from short-form sketches. He began posting on Instagram in 2017 as @Druski2funny, developing recurring characters and a deadpan record-label persona that anchors Coulda Been Records, the satirical label he launched in 2021 as an Instagram Live audition show and built into a touring and television property. He founded 4Lifers Entertainment in 2023 and took the Coulda Fest arena tour out in 2024, expanding it in 2025. Forbes ranked him No. 9 on its Top Creators list for 2025 with an estimated $14 million in earnings. CultureTechLens profiled Druski in Short #88, published October 13, 2026.

name: Duke Dennis
description: Duke Dennis (Denzel Dennis, born February 26, 1994, in Greenville, South Carolina) is an American streamer and content creator known for NBA 2K gameplay and as a founding member of the AMP (Any Means Possible) collective. Dennis served in the U.S. Army from 2013 to 2017, stationed in Germany, before building his channels on NBA 2K content beginning in 2016–2017. With AMP — formed in 2020 alongside Fanum, Agent 00, and ImDavisss, and later joined by Kai Cenat and Chrisnxtdoor — he became a central figure of the group's Atlanta streaming-house era. Rolling Stone named him to its list of the 25 most influential creators, and platform-reported figures in 2026 put his audience at roughly 3.5 million YouTube subscribers and 3.3 million Twitch followers. name: Desi Banks
description: Desi Banks is an Atlanta-based comedian, actor, and producer who moved from short-form Vine sketches, which he began posting in 2012, to headlining theaters and arenas. Banks built his audience on character sketches — Parlay, Lil Johnny, and Grandma Reese among them — rooted in Atlanta family life, began performing stand-up in 2017, and founded Desi Banks Productions to write, produce, and star in his own series and specials. His screen work includes Will Packer's Little (2019) alongside Regina Hall, Marsai Martin, and Issa Rae, the romantic comedy Love by Chance, and One of Them Days (2025). name: Dreezy
description: Seandrea Sledge (born March 28, 1994), known as Dreezy, is a rapper, singer and songwriter from Chicago's South Side. Raised moving between Chicago neighborhoods, she turned to singing, scatting and poetry as a child and began rapping at fourteen, citing J. Cole and Lil Wayne as influences. After early appearances with Sasha Go Hard and Lil Durk and the 2014 mixtape Schizo, her remix of “Chiraq” drew wide attention and a collaboration with Common. She signed with Interscope Records in 2014. Her debut album No Hard Feelings (2016) included “Body” featuring Jeremih, her first Billboard Hot 100 single, and “Close to You” featuring T-Pain. She followed with Big Dreez (2019) and acted as Queen Cabrini in the Netflix film Beats (2019). After leaving Interscope in 2020 and going independent, she released Hitgirl (2022), a collaboration with producer Hit-Boy, and the single “Bitch Duh” in 2024, sustaining a career that pairs sharp lyricism with R&B singing.

name: Deon Cole
description: Deon Cole, born Deon Anthony Cole on January 9, 1972, in the Roseland neighborhood of Chicago, Illinois, is an American comedian, actor, and screenwriter. He earned an acting degree from Philander Smith College in Little Rock, Arkansas, and began stand-up in Chicago after a friend bet him $50 that he would not get on stage. Cole joined the writing staff of The Tonight Show with Conan O'Brien in 2009 and Conan in 2010, sharing two Primetime Emmy nominations with the writing staff and three Writers Guild of America Award nominations. He played Charlie Telphy on the ABC sitcom Black-ish from 2014 to 2022, earning two NAACP Image Award nominations and two Screen Actors Guild Award nominations, and reprised the role on Grown-ish. He also starred as Detective Daniel “DJ” Tanner on Angie Tribeca and leads the BET+ drama Average Joe. His stand-up specials include Cole Blooded Seminar (2016), Cole Hearted (2019), Charleen's Boy (2022), and Ok, Mister (2024). In 2023 Philander Smith College awarded him an honorary doctorate.

name: Desmon Yancy
aliases: Desmon C. Yancy; Ald. Desmon Yancy
description: Desmon Yancy, born Desmon C. Yancy in 1971 or 1972 in Chicago, Illinois, is the alderperson of Chicago's 5th Ward, covering parts of Hyde Park, South Shore, Woodlawn, and Greater Grand Crossing. A Kenwood Academy graduate and the son of a Chicago police officer who served forty years, Yancy built his career as a labor organizer fighting for childcare and home-care workers and as senior director of organizing at the Inner-City Muslim Action Network. After the 2014 murder of Laquan McDonald he co-founded the Grassroots Alliance for Police Accountability in 2016, the coalition whose campaign produced the 2021 ordinance creating civilian oversight of the Chicago Police Department through the Community Commission for Public Safety and Accountability. Endorsed by retiring alderman Leslie Hairston, he won an eleven-candidate race and the April 2023 runoff with 6,184 votes (51.78 percent), taking office on May 15, 2023, on an anti-displacement platform centered on the neighborhoods surrounding the Obama Presidential Center.

name: David Moore
aliases: David H. Moore; Ald. David Moore
description: David Moore, born David H. Moore in Chicago, Illinois, is the alderman of Chicago's 17th Ward, covering parts of Englewood, Auburn Gresham, and Marquette Park. Raised in the Robert Taylor Homes and then in Englewood, he graduated from Simeon Vocational High School, earned a bachelor's degree in accounting and operations management from Western Illinois University, and a master's degree in government studies from Loyola University Chicago. He worked as an accountant for Fortune 500 companies, as a finance officer for the Chicago Department of Aviation, and as an assistant commissioner for the Cook County Board of Review. Moore traces his calling to walking the ward at age eleven with his uncle, an assistant precinct captain. He lost the 2011 aldermanic runoff to incumbent Latasha Thomas by roughly three hundred votes, won the open seat in 2015, and was sworn in on May 18, 2015. A member of the Council's Progressive Reform Caucus, he was re-elected in 2019 and 2023 and ran for Illinois secretary of state in 2022, finishing with under ten percent of the primary vote.

name: Don Thompson
description: Don Thompson, born Donald Thompson in 1963 in Chicago, Illinois, is an American business executive who became the first Black president and chief executive officer of McDonald's. Raised by his grandmother near Chicago's Cabrini-Green housing project — and from age eleven in Indianapolis, where he graduated from North Central High School — he earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from Purdue University and spent six years at the defense contractor Northrop Grumman. Recruited by McDonald's in 1990 as an engineer designing food-transport robotics and cooking controls, he crossed into operations through the company's accelerated development program, working restaurant floors and co-managing a South Side Chicago franchise. He rose to president of McDonald's USA in 2006, then chief operating officer, and on July 1, 2012, became president and CEO, the company's first African American chief executive. He led McDonald's until his retirement on March 1, 2015, and afterward founded the Chicago venture firm Cleveland Avenue, which invests in food, beverage, and related businesses.

name: Dee Brown
description: Dee Brown, born DeCovan Kadell Brown on November 29, 1968, in Jacksonville, Florida, is an American former professional basketball player and coach. A guard from Jacksonville University — where his No. 4 jersey was later retired — he was selected 19th overall by the Boston Celtics in the 1990 NBA draft. As a rookie he won the 1991 NBA Slam Dunk Contest with his famous no-look dunk, performed after pumping up his Reebok shoes, and was named to the NBA All-Rookie First Team. Brown played twelve NBA seasons — Boston (1990–1998), Toronto (1998–2000), and Orlando (2000–2002) — totaling 6,758 points, 2,227 assists, and 1,569 rebounds. He moved directly into coaching as head coach of the WNBA's Orlando Miracle (2002) and San Antonio Silver Stars (2004), then coached the Springfield Armor of the NBA Development League and served as an NBA assistant coach with the Detroit Pistons (2011–2013) and Sacramento Kings (2013–2015). His daughter Lexie Brown plays in the WNBA. This record documents the basketball player born in 1968; a younger guard of the same name (born 1984, Illinois) is a different person.

name: Dream Con
description: Dream Con is an annual multi-genre convention for anime, gaming and pop culture, founded in 2018 by the Texas comedy group RDCWorld (CTL-E-5605) after the group found established conventions unwelcoming to them as guests. The first edition drew about 800 people to Waco, Texas. Cancelled in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic, the convention resumed at Esports Stadium Arlington in 2021, moved to the Austin Convention Center in 2023, and in 2025 relocated to Houston's George R. Brown Convention Center, where it drew 32,674 paid attendees and a reported $19.2 million in economic impact — and where coverage describes it as the largest Black-owned anime and gaming convention in the United States. Dream Con 2026 returned to Houston with more than 30,000 attendees. RDCWorld's record in this graph has carried the convention as a named gap since the Shorts Wave 3 packet; this record is the event itself, minted on the festival precedent of the American Black Film Festival (CTL-E-5637).

name: DJ Spinderella
aliases: Deidra Roper; Deidra Muriel Roper; Spinderella
description: DJ Spinderella (born Deidra Roper on August 3, 1970, in Brooklyn, New York — some listings give 1971) is the DJ and producer who completed Salt-N-Pepa's classic lineup. Selected by producer Hurby 'Luv Bug' Azor in 1987, at sixteen, to replace the group's original DJ, she played on the trio's run of gold and platinum records, produced tracks on its albums, and shared its 1995 Grammy Award for Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group and its 2021 Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award. In January 2019 she was removed from the group's touring lineup; she stated publicly that she had received a termination email, and she sued James and Denton over royalties and contract claims. The case was resolved in a confidential settlement, and the trio later appeared together again, including the group's 2022 Hollywood Walk of Fame ceremony. On November 8, 2025, she was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame with Salt-N-Pepa — the first female DJ so honored — and in 2026 she told People the trio was 'in a good space' and touring together again.

name: DeRay Davis
description: DeRay Davis, born Antoine DeRay Davis on February 26, 1982, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American stand-up comedian and actor from the city's South Side. He built his act in Chicago clubs, broke through at Laffapalooza, and won Comedy Central's Laugh Riots, going on to Def Comedy Jam, ComicView, Comedy Central Presents, Showtime's Power Play, and the 2017 Netflix special How to Act Black. On screen he is best known as Ray “the Hustle Guy” in Barbershop (2002) and its sequels Barbershop 2 and The Next Cut, with further roles in 21 Jump Street and Semi-Pro and a recurring turn as Peaches on FX's Snowfall. Davis hosted the VH1 revival of Hip Hop Squares and the GSN game show Mind of a Man, is a regular on MTV's Wild 'n Out, and performed the skit voice work on Kanye West's albums The College Dropout and Late Registration. He hosts the “Mo Better Mondays” (Monderays) night at the Hollywood Improv.

name: Dewayne Perkins
description: Dewayne Perkins, born November 5, 1990, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American comedian, writer, actor, and producer. Raised on the South Side near Marquette Park, he graduated from Curie High School as its first Black male student to earn an International Baccalaureate diploma, and took his bachelor's degree at DePaul University after an early cut from its Theatre School redirected him to film and animation. Trained at The Second City and iO Theater, he formed the improv trio 3Peat, whose sketch “The Blackening” became a viral Comedy Central digital short in 2018. Perkins joined the writing staffs of The Break with Michelle Wolf, Brooklyn Nine-Nine — its only Black writer in season seven — the Saved by the Bell reboot, and The Amber Ruffin Show, which brought him a 2021 Primetime Emmy nomination for Outstanding Writing for a Variety Series. He co-wrote (with Tracy Oliver) and starred in the horror-comedy feature The Blackening, premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2022 and released in 2023, and has appeared on Wild 'n Out and The Upshaws.

name: Danitra Vance
description: Danitra Vance (July 13, 1954 – August 21, 1994) was an American comedian and actress born in Chicago, Illinois, and raised on the South Side. A Thornton Township High School graduate (1972) active in theater and debate, she graduated with honors from Roosevelt University and studied drama at London's Webber Douglas Academy of Dramatic Art. After performing with The Second City and becoming an Off-Broadway favorite, Vance joined Saturday Night Live for its eleventh season in 1985–86 as the first Black woman in the show's primary cast; her recurring work included the “That Black Girl” sketch and the character Cabrini Green Harlem Watts Jackson. She won an Obie Award and an NAACP Image Award, and appeared in the films Sticky Fingers (1988), Limit Up, and Jumpin' at the Boneyard. Diagnosed with breast cancer in 1990, she kept performing, including the solo piece The Radical Girl's Guide to Radical Mastectomy at the Joseph Papp Public Theater in 1991–93, and died in Markham, Illinois, on August 21, 1994, aged 40. As documented after her death, she was also among the first LGBT members of the SNL cast, though she was not publicly out in her lifetime.

name: Domo Wilson
description: Domo Wilson, born Dominique Wilson on June 24, 1994, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American YouTuber, singer, and social-media performer. Raised in Valparaiso, Indiana, after her family moved from Chicago, she began posting to YouTube in 2010 and built her following with comic short videos from 2014 onward, across Vine, Facebook, and YouTube. As a singer and songwriter she released her first single, “For You,” in 2014, followed by singles including “Feelings,” “Let's Do It,” and “Unbothered”; her most-viewed video is “Bisexual Anthem.” With her then-partner Crissy Danielle she ran the Domo and Crissy channels, launched September 2, 2019, which biography sources credit with nearly three million subscribers across their channels; the couple's son, Domonic, was born March 14, 2017. Wilson has also performed live music and comedy across the United States and delivered motivational talks in schools.

name: Doja Cat
aliases: Amala Ratna Zandile Dlamini; Amala Dlamini
description: Doja Cat, born Amala Ratna Zandile Dlamini on 21 October 1995 in Tarzana, Los Angeles, California, is an American rapper and singer signed to Kemosabe and RCA. After the debut EP Purrr! (2014) and the album Amala (2018), she broke virally with "Mooo!" in 2018. Hot Pink (2019) opened a run of pop-rap dominance; Planet Her (2021) reached No. 2 on the Billboard 200, and Scarlet (2023) followed. She won the Grammy for Best Pop Duo/Group Performance for "Kiss Me More" with SZA in 2022 — one win from nineteen nominations in the sourced count — and "Paint the Town Red" (2023) became her first solo Hot 100 No. 1. Her fifth album Vie was released 26 September 2025, debuting at No. 4 on the Billboard 200 with 57,000 first-week units, with the Tour Ma Vie world tour announced in October 2025.

name: DeVante Swing
aliases: Donald Earle DeGrate Jr.; Donald DeGrate Jr.; Mr. Dalvin (no — see notes)
description: DeVante Swing, born Donald Earle DeGrate Jr. on 29 September 1969 in Hampton, Virginia, and raised from Charlotte, North Carolina, is an American producer and songwriter, the founding architect of Jodeci. He formed the group with his brother Dalvin DeGrate and the Hailey brothers, K-Ci and JoJo — two pairs of brothers — and served as its main songwriter and producer. Signed to Uptown Records in 1989 after auditioning for Andre Harrell, Jodeci debuted with Forever My Lady (1991), written and produced largely by DeVante with Al B. Sure!. In 1991 he founded the Swing Mob collective, whose members included Timbaland, Missy Elliott, Magoo and Ginuwine. His outside production includes 2Pac's "No More Pain," and Jodeci reunited for The Past, the Present, the Future (2015).

name: Deion Sanders
aliases: Prime Time; Coach Prime; Deion Luwynn Sanders Sr.
description: Deion Luwynn Sanders Sr. (born August 9, 1967, in Fort Myers, Florida) is an American football coach and former professional football and baseball player. At Florida State he won the 1988 Jim Thorpe Award, and the Atlanta Falcons selected him fifth overall in the 1989 NFL draft. Across fourteen NFL seasons with Atlanta, San Francisco, Dallas, Washington and Baltimore he recorded 53 interceptions, earned eight Pro Bowl selections and was named the 1994 NFL Defensive Player of the Year; he won Super Bowl XXIX with the 49ers and Super Bowl XXX with the Cowboys, and was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2011. He also played nine Major League Baseball seasons, and is the only athlete to play in both a Super Bowl and a World Series, appearing in the 1992 World Series with Atlanta. As a coach he led Jackson State from 2020 to 2022, then became head coach at Colorado in 2023, where he coached his son Shedeur Sanders (CTL-E-5692) in 2023 and 2024 before Shedeur entered the 2025 NFL draft.

name: DeObia Oparei
description: DeObia Oparei, born 7 December 1971 in Hackney, London, to parents of Nigerian ancestry, is a British actor and playwright. Oparei began in British theatre, working with companies including the Royal Shakespeare Company and the National Youth Theatre, and made a film debut in Alien 3 before playing Le Chocolat in Baz Luhrmann's Moulin Rouge!. As a playwright, Oparei's first play opened at London's Royal Court Theatre in 2002 to critical acclaim and later toured to Sydney. Screen audiences know Oparei best for a run of large-scale productions: the Gunner in Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides (2011); Areo Hotah, captain of Prince Doran Martell's guard, in the fifth season of HBO's Game of Thrones (2015); Rongo in Tim Burton's Dumbo (2019); Mr. Effiong in Sex Education; and Boastful Loki in Marvel's Loki (2021), a role named in playful reference to an earlier character called Loki Hayes in Santa Clarita Diet. Rotten Tomatoes' filmography also credits roles in Independence Day: Resurgence, Jumanji: The Next Level, Wrath of Man and The Gray Man, a body of work built on physical presence and theatrical training.

name: Denny Love
description: Denny Love, born Denzel Irby on 30 December 1992 in Madison, Wisconsin, is an American actor and comedian whose route to television ran through Chicago. Raised in Madison and educated at Madison West High School, he studied acting at The Theatre School at DePaul University in Chicago, graduating with a BFA in 2015. His television debut came that same year on Chicago P.D., filmed in the city where he had trained, followed by a recurring role on Empire (2016–2017) and guest appearances including Lucifer. His breakthrough arrived in 2019 as Chip "The Colonel" Martin, the scholarship student at the emotional center of Hulu's eight-episode adaptation of John Green's novel Looking for Alaska, a lead role he has described pursuing with deliberate, written-down determination. He appeared in the film Unpregnant (2020) and joined Paramount+'s Mayor of Kingstown as rookie prison guard Kevin Jackson across its 2024–2025 seasons, a recurring run of thirteen episodes. In October 2026 he co-launched Saturday Morning Detention, a weekly YouTube comedy series, extending the panel-comedy work he had done on The Kevin Langue Show.

name: Dara Reneé
description: Dara Reneé, born Dara Reneé Brooks in Los Angeles, California, and raised in Baltimore, Maryland, is an American actress, singer and songwriter from a performing family: her mother, Kimberly Brooks, is an actress who founded a nonprofit performing-arts school, and her grandmother sang with the 1960s Baltimore soul group The Royalettes. Reneé made her screen debut as Savannah in Disney Channel's Freaky Friday (2018), then played Kourtney Greene across all four seasons of High School Musical: The Musical: The Series (2019–2023) on Disney+. She co-hosted Disney's Magic Bake-Off and, in 2024, stepped into the Descendants franchise as Uliana, younger sister of Ursula, in Descendants: The Rise of Red, a performance her biographical record credits with an Emmy Award nomination.

name: Doug Williams
description: Doug Williams (born August 9, 1955, in Zachary, Louisiana) is a former National Football League quarterback whose name is fixed to one of the landmark performances in American sports. At Grambling State University, playing for coach Eddie Robinson, he guided the Tigers to a 36-7 record as a four-year starter, won three Southwestern Athletic Conference championships, was twice named Black College Player of the Year, and finished fourth in the 1977 Heisman Trophy voting. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers selected him 17th overall in the 1978 NFL Draft, and he led Tampa Bay to the first three playoff appearances in team history. After two seasons in the USFL, he joined Washington in 1986. In Super Bowl XXII, on January 31, 1988, Williams threw for 340 yards and four touchdowns — all four in a single quarter — as Washington beat Denver 42-10. He was named Super Bowl MVP and became the first Black quarterback to both start and win a Super Bowl. Inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 2001, he later coached Grambling State and became a Washington team executive.

name: Désiré Doué
description: Désiré Doué, born on 3 June 2005 in Angers, France, is a French winger of Ivorian descent who plays for Paris Saint-Germain and the France national team. He joined Rennes as a child and made his senior debut in August 2022, becoming the first player born in 2005 to score in one of Europe's top five leagues. Paris Saint-Germain signed him in August 2024 on a five-year contract. He made his senior France debut in March 2025, and on 31 May 2025 he produced the defining performance of the Champions League final in Munich: two goals and an assist in PSG's 5–0 win over Inter Milan, the club's first European Cup, earning player of the match as the first teenager to score twice in a Champions League final. He was named the UEFA Champions League Young Player of the Season and won the 2025 Golden Boy award.

name: Dylan Harper
description: Dylan Harper, born Dylan Robert Harper on 2 March 2006 in New Jersey, is an American professional basketball player for the San Antonio Spurs. He is the son of Ron Harper, the five-time NBA champion guard, and Maria Pizarro Harper, who emigrated from Bataan in the Philippines at age seven, played Division I basketball at the University of New Orleans and coached her son from childhood through high school. A McDonald's All-American at Don Bosco Prep, Harper played one season at Rutgers, averaging 19.4 points, 4.6 rebounds and 4.0 assists and earning All-Big Ten honors. San Antonio selected him second overall in the 2025 NBA draft, making him one of the most prominent Filipino-descended players ever drafted. As a rookie he was named to the NBA All-Rookie First Team in 2026 and emerged as a key rotation guard in San Antonio's run to the 2026 NBA Finals, including a 24-point, 11-rebound, seven-steal game against Oklahoma City in the conference finals.

name: Devin Booker
description: Devin Booker, born Devin Armani Booker on 30 October 1996 in Grand Rapids, Michigan, is an American professional basketball player for the Phoenix Suns. The son of Melvin Booker, a former professional guard who starred at Missouri, and Veronica Gutierrez, he moved to Moss Point, Mississippi, to live with his father in high school and became a McDonald's All-American. After one season at Kentucky, where he was the Southeastern Conference Sixth Man of the Year, Phoenix drafted him 13th overall in 2015. At 20 he scored a franchise-record 70 points against Boston, the youngest player ever to score more than 60 in a game. He led Phoenix to the 2021 NBA Finals and earned All-NBA First Team honors in 2022. A five-time All-Star and a two-time Olympic gold medalist, he became the Suns' all-time leading scorer in February 2025. In June 2026 he changed his jersey from No. 1 to No. 15, his father's Missouri number, for the 2026-27 season.

name: Dennis Rodman
description: Dennis Rodman, born Dennis Keith Rodman on 13 May 1961 in Trenton, New Jersey, and raised in Dallas, Texas, is an American former forward regarded by NBA.com as arguably the best rebounding forward in the game's history. After a late growth spurt he starred at Southeastern Oklahoma State and was drafted by Detroit in the second round in 1986. With the Pistons' 'Bad Boys' he won championships in 1989 and 1990 and consecutive Defensive Player of the Year awards in 1990 and 1991. After two seasons in San Antonio he joined the Chicago Bulls in 1995 and completed their second three-peat, winning titles in 1996, 1997 and 1998 alongside Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen. He led the NBA in rebounds per game for a record seven consecutive seasons, made seven All-Defensive First Teams, and finished with 11,954 rebounds at 13.1 per game across fourteen seasons that closed with brief Lakers and Mavericks stops. Detroit retired his No. 10 jersey in 2011, and he was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame the same year and named to the NBA 75th Anniversary Team in 2021.

name: Damar Hamlin
description: Damar Hamlin, born Damar Romeyelle Hamlin on 24 March 1998 in McKees Rocks, Pennsylvania, is an American football safety for the Buffalo Bills. He attended Pittsburgh Central Catholic High School and played at the University of Pittsburgh, earning second-team All-ACC honors in 2020, before Buffalo selected him in the sixth round, 212th overall, of the 2021 NFL Draft. After a season as a backup he became a starter in 2022. On 2 January 2023, during a Monday Night Football game at Cincinnati, he suffered a cardiac arrest after making a tackle; his heartbeat was restored on the field, he was hospitalized in critical condition, and he was released from hospital nine days later. The episode was later attributed to commotio cordis, a rare disruption of the heart's rhythm caused by a blow to the chest. Cleared to play in April 2023, he returned during the 2023 season, started throughout 2024, and became a national advocate for CPR training and AED access through his Chasing M's Foundation. Buffalo re-signed him on a one-year deal in March 2026 for the 2026 season.

name: Dorothy Height
description: Dorothy Height (Dorothy Irene Height, born March 24, 1912, Richmond, Virginia; died April 20, 2010, Washington, D.C., aged 98) was, in the phrase attached to her across the movement, its godmother. Raised in Rankin, Pennsylvania, she was admitted to Barnard College in 1929 and turned away under its quota for Black students; she took her bachelor's in education and her master's in psychology at New York University instead. On the Harlem YWCA staff she pushed the YWCA's national integration and founded its Center for Racial Justice. In 1937 she met Mary McLeod Bethune and joined the National Council of Negro Women, becoming its fourth president in 1957 and holding the post for forty years, until 1997. She helped organize the 1963 March on Washington — she sat on its platform, though the program gave her no speech — and ran the Wednesdays in Mississippi project joining Northern and Southern women. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1994 and the Congressional Gold Medal in 2004.

name: David Ortiz
aliases: David Américo Ortiz Arias; Big Papi
description: David Américo Ortiz Arias, born 18 November 1975 in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, is an Afro-Dominican designated hitter known worldwide as “Big Papi.” Released by the Minnesota Twins after the 2002 season, he signed with the Boston Red Sox and became the most feared clutch hitter of his generation: a ten-time All-Star who powered Boston to World Series championships in 2004 — ending the franchise's 86-year drought — 2007 and 2013, when he batted .688 and was named World Series MVP. He retired after 2016 with 541 home runs, 2,472 hits and a .286 career average, the greatest designated-hitter résumé in history. In 2022 he was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame on the first ballot with 77.9 percent of the vote, the fourth Dominican-born player so honored. He became a U.S. citizen in 2008 and founded the David Ortiz Children's Fund for pediatric cardiac care in Boston and the Dominican Republic.

name: David Kellum
description: David Kellum was a leading Chicago Defender figure from the 1920s through the 1950s whose work ran through the paper's youth pages. Chicago Public Library's Harsh Research Collection holds his papers and credits him with a central role in the Bud Billiken enterprise: he became editor of the Defender Junior children's section in 1927 and, with publisher Robert S. Abbott and editor Lucius Harper, developed the idea of an annual Defender-sponsored parade honoring the paper's newsboys. That parade, first held in 1929, grew into the Bud Billiken Parade, the largest African American parade in the United States and a back-to-school institution on Chicago's South Side. Kellum served as an early coordinator of the parade, and his surviving papers — photographs and an oral history recorded with his son — preserve the Billiken world of contests, clubs, and Washington Park picnics that organized Black Chicago childhood for a generation.

name: Devin Haney
description: Devin Haney, born Devin Miles Haney on 17 November 1998 in San Francisco, California, is an American professional boxer who has won world championships in three weight classes. Raised in Oakland and Las Vegas and trained by his father, Bill Haney, he turned professional at seventeen in Mexico because he was too young to be licensed in the United States. He won the WBC lightweight title in 2019 and became the undisputed lightweight champion in 2022 by defeating George Kambosos Jr. in Australia, then defended that status in a rematch and against Vasiliy Lomachenko. Moving up, he took the WBC super lightweight title from Regis Prograis in December 2023. After his April 2024 fight with Ryan Garcia was ruled a no contest, Haney won the WBO welterweight title from Brian Norman Jr. in November 2025, and in October 2026 he remained champion while a proposed superfight with Shakur Stevenson stalled over weight terms.

name: Deontay Wilder
aliases: Deontay Leshun Wilder; The Bronze Bomber
description: Deontay Wilder, born Deontay Leshun Wilder on 22 October 1985 in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, is an American professional heavyweight boxer. He began boxing at twenty to support his young family, including a daughter born with spina bifida, and within three years had won the National Golden Gloves, the United States championships and a bronze medal at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, the result behind his Bronze Bomber nickname. Turning professional in 2008, he built a long knockout streak before defeating Bermane Stiverne in January 2015 to win the WBC heavyweight title, becoming the first American world heavyweight champion since 2007. He defended the title ten times, including a drawn first fight with Tyson Fury in 2018, before losing it to Fury in 2020 and losing their 2021 trilogy bout. After defeats by Joseph Parker and Zhilei Zhang, he returned with wins in 2025 and a split-decision victory over Derek Chisora in London in April 2026.

name: Damon Wayans
aliases: Damon Kyle Wayans; Damon Wayans Sr.
description: Damon Wayans, born Damon Kyle Wayans on 4 September 1960 in New York City, is an American stand-up comedian, actor and writer, and a central member of the Wayans family of entertainers. One of ten children raised in Harlem, he began stand-up in 1982 and served a brief, famously turbulent stint as a featured player on Saturday Night Live in 1985–86. His breakthrough came as a writer and performer on Fox's In Living Color (1990–1992), created by his brother Keenen Ivory Wayans, where his characters — including Homey the Clown and the 'Men on Film' critic Blaine Edwards — became signature figures of Black sketch comedy. He headlined films including Mo' Money, Major Payne and Spike Lee's Bamboozled, starred as Michael Kyle in the ABC sitcom My Wife and Kids (2001–2005) and as Roger Murtaugh in the Lethal Weapon television series (2016–2019), and in 2024 co-created and starred in the CBS sitcom Poppa's House alongside his son, Damon Wayans Jr. In February 2025 the Wayans family was inducted into the NAACP Image Awards Hall of Fame.

name: DJ Kool Herc
description: DJ Kool Herc, born Clive Campbell on April 16, 1955, in Kingston, Jamaica, is a Jamaican American disc jockey credited by Britannica as the founder of hip-hop. Campbell immigrated to the Bronx in 1967, and his family settled at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue. On August 11, 1973, his sister Cindy Campbell hosted a back-to-school party in the building's recreation room and hired her brother to deejay. There he introduced his two-turntable technique, which he called the merry-go-round, using two copies of the same record to loop the percussive breaks in funk songs and extend the passages dancers loved, while calling out dancers he named B-boys and B-girls. Music historians credit the innovations at that party with providing the foundation for hip-hop, and August 11, 1973, is now considered the music's birth date. Herc's style influenced Afrika Bambaataa and Grandmaster Flash. He stopped performing after a 1977 stabbing, appeared in the 1984 film Beat Street, and was recognized by Congress in 2021. The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inducted him in 2023.

name: Dorothy Tucker
description: Dorothy Tucker is a Chicago native, raised in the city's Lawndale and Austin communities, who has been a reporter for CBS 2 Chicago since 1984 and serves on the station's 2 Investigators team. She began her broadcasting career in Peoria at WMBD-TV, after serving as an intern at CBS 2 Chicago in 1977, and worked at WREG-TV in Memphis in 1979-80, at KWGN-TV in Denver, and at KDKA-TV in Pittsburgh, where she was a general assignment reporter and talk show host, before joining CBS 2. She graduated with honors from Northwestern University with a B.S. in Communications. In August 2019 the National Association of Black Journalists elected her its 22nd president; she had previously served on the NABJ board as Region V Director and as Vice President-Broadcast, and she is a local board member of NABJ-Chicago. Her honors include several local Emmys, two regional Edward R. Murrow Awards in 2021, and a Chicago Headline Club Lifetime Achievement Award. In 2024 the station marked her 40th year at CBS News Chicago with a special tribute.

name: Dorie Miller
description: Doris Miller, known as Dorie, was a United States Navy sailor born October 12, 1919, in Waco, Texas, where he grew up on his family's farm and played high-school football. He enlisted in 1939 as a mess attendant, one of the few roles then open to African Americans, and in 1940 was assigned to the battleship USS West Virginia at Pearl Harbor, where he became the ship's heavyweight boxing champion. On December 7, 1941, after a torpedo strike damaged his battle station, he helped carry the ship's mortally wounded captain to safety, then loaded and fired an anti-aircraft machine gun he had never been trained to operate, and stayed to help evacuate shipmates after the order to abandon ship. He became the first African American awarded the Navy Cross, presented by Admiral Chester Nimitz on May 27, 1942. Promoted to cook third class, he was later assigned to the escort carrier USS Liscome Bay, and died November 24, 1943, when a torpedo sank that ship off the Gilbert Islands, at age twenty-four.

name: Data for Black Lives
description: Data for Black Lives (D4BL) is a movement organization founded in 2017 by Yeshimabeit Milner, with Lucas Mason-Brown as co-founder, to use data science to create concrete and measurable change in the lives of Black people. It began publicly with its inaugural conference at the MIT Media Lab on November 17–19, 2017, organized by Mason-Brown, Milner, and Max Clermont, which drew hundreds of scientists, mathematicians, technologists, and community activists, with hundreds more on a waiting list. Milner, who leads the organization as its founder and chief executive, frames its work as turning data from a weapon of political oppression into a tool for social change; its signature campaign, Abolish Big Data, calls for dismantling the structures that concentrate data power and putting data in the hands of the people who need it most. The organization has campaigned against predictive policing, risk-based sentencing, and predatory lending, built a COVID-19 database tracking the pandemic's impact on Black communities, and grown, by the JFK Library's account, to more than 4,000 members while raising over $2 million.

name: Da'Vine Joy Randolph
description: Da'Vine Joy Randolph is an American actress born May 21, 1986, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and raised in the city's Mount Airy neighborhood. She studied classical vocal performance and opera at Temple University, switching to musical theatre in her junior year and graduating in 2008, then earned a master's degree from the Yale School of Drama in 2011, with a summer studying Shakespeare at Oxford through the British American Drama Academy. She gained recognition as Oda Mae Brown in the Broadway production of Ghost in 2012, receiving a nomination for the Tony Award for Best Featured Actress in a Musical, and made her feature film debut in Mother of George in 2013. Screen roles followed in Dolemite Is My Name in 2019 and The United States vs. Billie Holiday in 2021, alongside television work including Only Murders in the Building from 2021. In 2023 she played Mahalia Jackson in Rustin and Mary Lamb, a school cook and bereaved mother, in The Holdovers. The Holdovers performance won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress at the 2024 ceremony, together with the Golden Globe, BAFTA, and Screen Actors Guild awards, and in 2024 she received a Primetime Emmy nomination and was named to the Time 100 list.

name: Don Lemon
description: Don Lemon is an American journalist born March 1, 1966, in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. He attended Louisiana State University and graduated from Brooklyn College in 1996 with a degree in broadcast journalism, interning at WNYW while a student. He worked as a weekend anchor and reporter at stations in Birmingham, Philadelphia, St. Louis, and Chicago, and as a correspondent for NBC News programs including Today and NBC Nightly News, before working at NBC's WMAQ-TV in Chicago from 2003. He joined CNN in September 2006 as a correspondent and became host of the prime-time program that became Don Lemon Tonight, which he anchored from 2014 to 2022. In late 2022 he moved to co-anchor CNN This Morning with Kaitlan Collins and Poppy Harlow. CNN fired him in April 2023. His reporting honors include an Edward R. Murrow Award in 2002 for coverage of the capture of the Washington, D.C. snipers and three regional Emmy Awards earned in Chicago. His memoir Transparent was published in 2011. In January 2024 he announced The Don Lemon Show as an independent program, which continues outside CNN.

name: Donovan McNabb
description: Donovan Jamal McNabb is a former American football quarterback born November 25, 1976, in Chicago, Illinois. Raised in Chicago, he attended Mount Carmel High School, where he helped the team win the 1991 state championship as a sophomore and a Chicago Prep Bowl championship as a senior. At Syracuse University he started every game after redshirting in 1994, was named Big East Offensive Player of the Year three times from 1996 to 1998, and also played as a reserve on the Syracuse basketball team. The Philadelphia Eagles selected him second overall in the 1999 NFL draft. As the Eagles' starting quarterback from 1999 to 2009 he led the team to eight playoff appearances, five NFC Championship Games, and Super Bowl XXXIX, and became the franchise leader in passing yards, passing touchdowns, attempts, and completions. He spent one season each with Washington in 2010 and Minnesota in 2011, was selected to six Pro Bowls, and was inducted into the Philadelphia Eagles Hall of Fame in 2013, when the team retired his number 5.

name: Double V campaign
description: The Double V campaign was a Black American campaign led by the Pittsburgh Courier during World War II, launched on February 7, 1942. It took its name and program from a letter by James G. Thompson, a 26-year-old reader, published by the Courier on January 31, 1942, which asked whether he should sacrifice to live half American and proposed a double V: victory over enemies from without and victory over enemies from within. The Courier built the campaign around two linked demands, victory in the war abroad and victory against discrimination at home, including fighting the poll tax and disfranchisement, equality in education, and equal opportunity in the defense industry, while urging support for the war effort through war bonds, blood banks, and conservation. The campaign spread from Pittsburgh to Black communities across the country, where local Double V clubs formed and supporters wore Double V pins. The organized campaign faded by 1943, but Black newspapers continued to advance its ideals, and it is often treated as an early part of the civil rights movement.

name: Dorothy Jenkins Fields
aliases: Dr. Dorothy Jenkins Fields; Dorothy Fields
description: Dorothy Jenkins Fields is a historian, archivist, and preservationist who founded the Black Archives, History and Research Foundation of South Florida, Inc. in Miami in 1977. She began gathering the history of African Americans in Miami-Dade County in 1974, after finding the original city charter listing the Black and white men who voted to incorporate Miami on July 28, 1896, while searching for curriculum as a young teacher preparing for the United States Bicentennial. She went on to earn a certification in archives administration and a Ph.D. in twentieth-century African American history, historic preservation, and public history. The Black Archives she created is a nonprofit manuscript and photographic repository for the legacies of Miami's Black community, covering the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and collecting photographs, documents, and oral histories from people who lived through the Jim Crow era and beyond. The foundation was also the catalyst for her campaign to preserve the Lyric Theater and other historic sites in Overtown; the theater was restored and reopened in 1999. In 2024 she was named a 2024–2025 Creative Futures Fellow by the University of Miami's Center for Global Black Studies, after fifty years of preservation work.

name: Destiny Singleton
description: Destiny Singleton serves as the 2025–2026 Honorary Student Board Member of the Chicago Board of Education, the student seat that represents the interests and perspectives of all Chicago Public Schools students at Board meetings; the Board's official agenda of action records her term as June 26, 2025 to June 25, 2026. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026. This record carries honor and role facts only.

name: Dixon Romeo
description: Dixon Romeo is the inaugural Executive Director of Southside Together, the South Side Chicago community-organizing organization formed by the merger of STOP and Not Me We — the latter of which he co-founded and previously led as Executive Director. The organization continues that work on housing, health, youth, education and mutual aid across Woodlawn, South Shore, Greater Grand Crossing and Park Manor, including tenant-union organizing, and 2025 coverage still cites him in the role. He was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.
